title: perceptual-value-pricing-scratchpad
content:
Perceptual value pricing — scratchpad (notes to self / rough math)

Goal: explore a pricing primitive that charges for the *user-perceived* value (latency + quality + context length) rather than raw tokens alone. Try to keep a simple conversion to USD via GPU-hour amortization so we can sketch product tiers. This is exploratory; lots of heuristics below.

Key idea: create a small set of "value buckets" (V1/V2/V3) where each bucket maps to an effective token cost multiplier. Buckets are determined by runtime SLO (p95 latency), model family (FP32/quantized), and effective context length used.

Definitions (working):
- GPU-hour amortized cost: all infra + ops + cooling + amortization per GPU-hour (placeholder input).
- Throughput (tokens/hr): depends heavily on batchability and request size distribution. Use three service modes: interactive, balanced, batch.
- Base token cost = GPU-hour-cost / tokens-per-hour.
- Perceptual multiplier = factor applied to base cost for a given V-bucket (captures value of low latency and long context).

Assumptions (pick sensible defaults for back-of-envelope):
- GPU-hour amortized cost (a) = $4.50 /GPU-hour (includes infra + idle overhead + ops). (Experiment with $3–$9 range later.)
- Throughput (tokens/hr):
  * Interactive (I): 400k tokens/hr (small requests, low batching)
  * Balanced (B): 1.08M tokens/hr (typical mixed traffic)
  * Batch (X): 5.0M tokens/hr (large-batch scoring jobs)
- Therefore base cost per 1k tokens:
  * I: $4.5 / 400k * 1000 = $0.01125 per 1k tokens
  * B: $4.5 / 1.08M * 1000 ≈ $0.00417 per 1k tokens
  * X: $4.5 / 5.0M * 1000 = $0.00090 per 1k tokens
- Add 20% product/engineering overhead and 30% gross margin target on top of base to get price floor for public-facing tiers.

Perceptual multipliers (conceptual):
- V1 (latency-critical, short-turn): multiplier 3.0 (prioritize p95 < 300ms, keep hot KV cache)
- V2 (balanced UX): multiplier 1.25 (p95 ~ 300–800ms)
- V3 (cost-optimized, batch): multiplier 0.6 (no latency guarantees, high batching)
(These are starting points; need empirical calibration.)

Example prices (apply overhead + margin then perceptual multiplier):
- Start with Balanced base price (incl overhead+margin): base_B_price = $0.00417 * 1.2 * 1.3 ≈ $0.0065 per 1k tokens
- V1 (interactive) price per 1k = base_B_price * 3.0 ≈ $0.0195 per 1k tokens
- V2 price per 1k = base_B_price * 1.25 ≈ $0.0081 per 1k tokens
- V3 price per 1k = base_B_price * 0.6 ≈ $0.0039 per 1k tokens

Session-level examples (to make product-friendly offerings):
- Typical conversational session = 600 tokens prompt + 400 tokens generation = 1k tokens total.
  * V1 session cost ≈ $0.0195 (so 50 sessions ≈ $0.975)
  * V2 session cost ≈ $0.0081 (50 sessions ≈ $0.405)
- Long-context analysis (10k tokens roundtrip) at V2 ≈ 10 * $0.0081 = $0.081 per request.

Tier sketches (product ideas):
- Freemium: 7-day trial credits, V3-only access, throttle concurrency.
- Starter (payg): $0.009 / 1k tokens (V2-equivalent floor), soft concurrency limits, community support.
- Team (committed): commit $X/mo -> discount to V2 base with included burst credits in V1 for short durations. Example: commit $500/mo -> 15% discount on V2, plus 10k V1-value credits.
- Enterprise SLO-backed: per-seat or per-commit pricing with defined V1 capacity SLA. Private deployments priced as a managed recurring fee + per-usage V1/V2/V3 accounting.

Credentialing / Credits model idea:
- Instead of raw tokens, sell "value credits" (VC) where 1 VC = 1 unit of V2 1k-token equivalent.
- Customers buy VC packages; using V1 consumes 3 VC per 1k token, V3 consumes 0.6 VC per 1k token.
- Pack sizing: round numbers (10k VC, 100k VC) with expiration windows (rolling 12 months or 30-day decays).
- Seat-level or key-level policies: per-key throttle on V1 consumption to prevent noisy neighbor burst consumption.

Open questions / risks (todo list):
- How to measure and tag a request as V1/V2/V3 reliably? (client hint + server-side heuristics).
- UX: avoid surprising customers with multipliers. Make credit consumption visible in console per-request.
- Billing complexity: adding 3-tier multipliers increases billing noise. Need clear invoice line items and tooling in Console.
- Discount math: how to translate commit discounts into effective VC price while preserving margin?
- Attack surface: could customers spoof hints to avoid V1 pricing. Need server-side enforcement (latency SLA + queueing policy).

Calcs to validate next (actionable):
1) Re-run base GPU-hour numbers for our model catalog (Llama-2-13B, 70B quantized) — ask infra for measured tokens/hr at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 token/sec per-request distributions. (Slack: #infra-costs)
2) Simulate 10k customers with mixes (60% small interactive, 30% balanced, 10% batch) to see revenue vs cost curves across commit levels.
3) UX trial: instrument Console to surface a per-request "VC burn rate" in the low-fidelity prototype.

Prototype pricing scenarios to run (quick experiments):
- Scenario A: Low-touch startups (monthly $0–500): default access to V2 and V3, payg top-up. Expect high variance; cap V1 to 5% of total VC by default.
- Scenario B: Growth teams ($2k–$15k/mo): include monthly VC pool, allow reserved V1 slots for on-call support and canary tests.
- Scenario C: Enterprise ($50k+/mo commit): guarantee X% V1 capacity across region, charge uplift for private deployments to cover ops.

UX language drafts (short):
- "Value Credits (VC): One VC equals the cost-equivalent of 1k tokens on our standard balanced runtime. High-priority, low-latency requests consume more VC. You can buy VC packs or commit monthly for discounts."
- Keep it simple: show meters "VC remaining" and two toggles on the Console: "Performance hints (auto)" and "Force cost-optimized".

Next steps (this doc):
- Clean up numbers (talk to infra on actual tokens/hr) and create a simple simulator (spreadsheet or notebook).
- Draft a one-pager (internal) to share with product and infra.
- Prototype Console meters + sample invoice line layout.

Random scribbles / heuristics:
- Consider time-of-day multipliers for spare capacity (cheap nights for batch scoring).
- Explore commit tiers expressed in VC/day rather than VC/mo for usage forecasting.
- Evaluate whether a short-term V1 burst bucket (pre-paid ephemeral credits) reduces purchase friction.

References / reminders: link pricing experiments in drive + previous scratchpads (TODO reconcile with commit vs payg buckets). Also ping @ops for GPU amortization numbers.

-- E.Z.
